title: Concurrency and memory-throttling: SKU contrast across A100/H100/L40S
content:
Purpose:
Quick working exploration of how concurrent decode workers interact with per-GPU memory-eviction/throttling behavior across cloud SKUs (A100/H100/L40S) and driver/CUDA versions. Goal is to surface reproducible signals that explain sudden per-token latency inflation at higher concurrency and to identify short-term mitigation knobs for Dedicated and Hosted routing layers.

Background/context:
- Several customer incidents in Q2–Q3 revealed transient p50->p99 amplification when multiple short requests hit the same GPU (small prompts, bursty concurrency). Symptoms look like memory reclamation stalls and kernel-launch contention rather than pure compute saturation.
- Prior docs covered occupancy, KV-cache repopulation, and power/clock throttling; this note focuses on the interplay between concurrency (# of decode streams), per-GPU resident memory pressure, and driver-initiated reclamation (eviction / CC cache compaction) across SKUs.

Hypothesis:
1) At moderate concurrency (8–16 streams) certain driver+CUDA combos trigger background housekeeping (GC-like or ECC scrubbing) that pauses scheduling or increases kernel launch latency, exacerbated on SKUs with smaller HBM per-GPU or tighter memory allocator fragmentation (e.g., A100 40GB vs H100 80GB).
2) L40S behaves differently due to different firmware and memory management; it may show lower p50 but higher p99 when KV-cache churn is high.
3) Differences between cloud provider SKUs (placement, PCIe vs NVLink topology) affect inter-stream contention and visible latency spikes.

Testbed and measurement plan (quick matrix):
- SKUs: A100 40GB (n1), A100 80GB (n2), H100 80GB, L40S 48GB (where available)
- Providers/instances: aws.p4d (A100 40GB), gcp.a2-highgpu-1 (A100 80GB), aws.hpc6a-h100 (H100), azure.l40s-v3 (L40S)
- Driver/CUDA: driver combos tested: (520/11.8), (535/12.1), (534/12.2), (554/12.3) — chosen based on region availability
- Model: rw-deploy-test-7B (decoder-only) with KV-cache enabled; smaller prompt sizes (16 tokens prefill, 64 decode target) to emphasize short requests
- Concurrency sweep: 1, 4, 8, 16, 32 streams (steady-state for 300s per point)
- Workload: each stream issues sequential requests with 200ms inter-request gap to simulate real bursty PLG traffic; warmups run until KV-cache stabilized
- Metrics captured: p50/p95/p99 per-token latency, kernel-launch latency histogram (via CUPTI/tooling), GPU memory allocated/fragmentation snapshot, ECC/errors, PCIe/NVLink utilization, cpu-side queueing, dcgm counters for memory_free and memory_used, dmesg/kernel logs for driver events

Methodology notes:
- Use isolated single-GPU instances where possible to remove multi-tenant noise. For multi-tenant/multi-GPU tests we pin all streams to single device for parity.
- Capture perf traces and a light ebpf trace for kernel launches on host to attempt to correlate host-scheduling stalls with GPU kernel gaps.
- Reproduce each combination 3x and report median, with outlier annotations.
- Use deterministic seed for model to make token lengths comparable.

Results summary (high level):
- A100 40GB (driver 535/CUDA 12.1): p50 remains flat up to 8 streams; p95 increases 1.6x at 16 streams; p99 shows sharp cliff at 32 streams. Kernel-launch hysteresis (50–200ms) visible in CUPTI traces at 16+ streams, correlated with short windows of memory fragmentation and small spikes in driver GC events.
- A100 80GB (driver 534/CUDA 12.2): more headroom; p99 still grows but smoothly; kernel launch gaps are smaller and less frequent. Memory snapshots show lower fragmentation and more successful KV-cache pinning.
- H100 80GB (driver 554/CUDA 12.3): best tail behaviour at mid concurrency (8–16), but at 32 streams p99 jumps similar to A100 40GB. Observed occasional firmware-level telemetry events (therm/power governor transitions) on sustained bursts that coincide with per-token latency spikes.
- L40S 48GB (driver 520/CUDA 11.8): surprisingly low p50 at high concurrency but p99 worse than A100 80GB. Kernel latency histograms show many small micro-gaps (~10–30ms) rather than large pauses; suggests faster but more frequent scheduler preemption.

Representative numbers (median of 3 runs) — model decode token latency (ms):
- A100-40: concurrency 1 -> p50 5.2 p99 12.7; concurrency 16 -> p50 6.1 p99 78.9; concurrency 32 -> p50 7.0 p99 220.
- A100-80: concurrency 1 -> p50 5.3 p99 11.9; concurrency 16 -> p50 6.0 p99 34.2; concurrency 32 -> p50 6.8 p99 95.
- H100-80: concurrency 1 -> p50 4.8 p99 10.5; concurrency 16 -> p50 5.5 p99 29.0; concurrency 32 -> p50 6.3 p99 180.
- L40S-48: concurrency 1 -> p50 4.9 p99 14.3; concurrency 16 -> p50 5.6 p99 65.1; concurrency 32 -> p50 6.0 p99 210.

Notes on driver/CUDA differences:
- Driver 535 on A100-40 showed a specific pattern: background memory compaction tasks reported in driver logs coincident with kernel launch gaps. Switching to 534 removed most of the long pauses for the same workload.
- Newer drivers (554) on H100 exposed power governor transitions under synthetic steady bursts (not always seen in cloud telemetry) — correlates with temporary clock downshifts that hurt tail latency.

Observed causes and interpretation:
- Two main root causes surfaced: (a) host-side kernel launch contention and scheduling jitter (likely from driver housekeeping or long syscalls); (b) firmware/thermals/power governor transitions under sustained burst patterns causing frequency drops.
- Memory fragmentation contributes by forcing allocator to do more frequent device allocations/frees (KV-cache churn), which can trigger the driver’s background compaction or reclamation path. This is most visible on smaller-HBM SKUs.
- L40S tends to favor frequent preemption rather than rare long stalls; this yields better p50 but worse p99 under heavy churn. H100’s extra HBM gives headroom but is subject to firmware-level protections that can create long tails under certain workloads.

Mitigations tried (short experiments):
- Pre-reserving KV cache: pinning large resident buffers at startup reduced fragmentation events and dropped p99 by ~30% on A100-40.
- Slightly increasing inter-request backoff (from 200ms to 350ms) smoothed p99 across all SKUs but reduces peak throughput — candidate for Hosted adaptive throttling.
- Driver rollback to 534 on A100-40 removed large kernel-launch pauses in our testbed. Risk: older driver misses other fixes; needs regression testing.
- Firmware/BIOS tuning on H100 (clock governor policy) helped in lab but not available in cloud-managed SKUs.

Open questions and follow-ups:
- Are driver GC/compaction events observable via public DCGM counters or only in driver logs requiring support from cloud vendor? Need cloud support tickets for better telemetry.
- Does multi-GPU colocated tenancy amplify the effect (we tested single-GPU isolates); schedule a small matrix to validate multi-tenant interference.
- Can the runtime reduce per-request allocation churn by pooling decoded KV slices more aggressively? Design proposal: persistent pooling with soft-LRU eviction instead of per-request allocate/free. Evaluate memory overhead vs tail improvements.
- For Dedicated customers, expose an opt-in conservative allocator/kv-pin mode in the runtime (config flag) to improve p99 on smaller-HBM SKUs.

Action items:
- [Samir] file cloud provider tickets requesting driver logs/DCGM access for background compaction events (due 2025-02-10).
- [Alex] prototype persistent KV pool patch and bench at concurrency 16/32 across A100/H100 (due 2025-03-01).
- [Maya] draft Hosted adaptive throttling experiment design (backoff policy + capacity routing) and run 2-week canary on low-traffic region (due 2025-02-20).
- [Priya] run multi-tenant single-host noisy-neighbor matrix (1 co-tenant busy stream + our test) and report delta (due 2025-02-28).

Repro notes (how to run the primary experiment):
1) Start clean VM with pinned driver version per test row. Reboot to ensure kernel modules are fresh.
2) Build runtime with CUPTI tracing enabled and light ebpf host-sampler.
3) Deploy model container, warm for 600s with low-rate requests to populate KV cache.
4) Run concurrency harness for 300s per point, capture dcgm, dmesg, CUPTI, and host ebpf traces.
5) Aggregate via our perf-collector script and run the analysis notebook (link in PR).

Appendix: quick heuristics for product teams
- If using A100-40 and seeing p99 cliffs at ~16+ concurrency, try driver 534 or enable kv-pin in runtime as short-term mitigation.
- For Hosted, implement simple adaptive backoff when p99 > threshold for a route (this buys time to reroute to larger SKUs without customer-visible errors).
- For Dedicated/Private, prioritize H100 80GB or A100 80GB for heavy small-request workloads; L40S ok for p50-focused workloads but expect tail risk.
